analysisDescription: Tried to read all the options and see what fits best. There where some mecanics of the game that were hard to explain with the framework alone and where complemented with the comments.

dimension.title: Party Creation
dimension.description: Party Creation encompasses all games where groups are defined by the players themselves prior to initiating gameplay, typically leveraging friend lists or co-located party creation.

dimensionExamples.example: The main goal of the game is to gather scrap to meet the quota in order to survive. All players have this goal and they either all succeed or all fail.

dimension.title: Shared
dimension.description: Shared goals consist of singular objectives that multiple players pursue and work together to achieve

dimensionExamples.example: The progression is tied to a save file that usually the host keeps. The host can later reload this save and play with the same or a different team

dimension.title: Server
dimension.description: Server progression is defined by the existence of persistent mutable worlds that a number of players share. The action of players (i.e. collaborating or not) can impact the overall progression/evolution of the game world, affecting others.

dimension.title: Single
dimension.description: Single applies to any game where players have control of one single entity.

dimension.title: Distinct
dimension.description: Distinct means that each player controls a different entity or set of entities

dimension.title: Arbitrary
dimension.description: Arbitrary means that all player entities are equal in their ability to act upon the world. If a selection exists, it is merely an aesthetic choice.

dimensionExamples.example: The player's entity does not change all the game beside being able to choose basic colors as cosmetic

dimension.title: Static
dimension.description: When the player's entity is constant throughout gameplay.

dimensionExamples.example: All players are part of the same team with the same objective

dimension.title: Teammates
dimension.description: Teammates, where players within a team need to coordinate their actions, abilities, and roles in order to reach a common goal against at least another team.

dimensionExamples.example: The world is the same for all players differing only in where the player is or is looking at. If the players wish so, it is possible for the players to always stick together and see the same things.

dimension.title: Shared
dimension.description: Shared world views apply to a game when players have access to the same world.

dimension.title: Distinct
dimension.description: Distinct refers to when each player has control of their own individual viewpoint, typically through separate screens.

dimensionExamples.example: The only goal the game gives is to "gather scrap", players are free to do what they want in order to try and complete the objective.

dimension.title: Free Collaboration
dimension.description: In free collaboration, players can take on available tasks as they wish and decide how to contribute.

dimension.title: Concurrent Collaboration
dimension.description: In concurrent collaboration, players have to perform gameplay tasks concurrently.

dimensionExamples.example: By definition the game is meant to be played using the in game voice chat. This voice chat is proximity based and besides it there arent many ways to communicate. Another limitation to this is that dead players cannot communicate with players alive. All of these limit the flow of information by a lot.

dimension.title: Limited
dimension.description: When Limited, the game restricts communication, while not prohibiting it as a whole. It can be achieved through gameplay mechanics such as designated time/space when communication is allowed, or through allowing communication through only specific modalities only (e.g. pings, emotes); or through rules that the players should follow (e.g. do not communicate your exact position).

dimensionExamples.example: The primary way to communicate with other players.

dimension.title: Voice Chat
dimension.description: Support for players to communicate using their voice

dimensionExamples.example: An alternative way for players to express themselfs through the moviment combined with speech.

dimension.title: In-Game Movement/Actions
dimension.description: Players can communicate through specific movement or actions (e.g. shooting a weapon on the ground to notify others to pick it up)

dimensionExamples.example: A game "round" bases itself on a day and as the day progresses, it will become harder until the day ends and the round forcibly ends

dimension.title: Temporal
dimension.description: Temporal, when there are temporal dependent events that affect both players. For example, ensuring action concurrencies or timing.

dimensionExamples.example: There is a way to directly act as an assistant to other players altough that is not forced nor is present during the whole game.

dimension.title: Assistive Actions
dimension.description: Assistive Actions encompass actions that one player performs to the benefit of other/s (i.e. note that the player can have indirect benefits such as reviving others to increase their own chances of success). In these games, players can support and assist other players in achieving their objectives.

dimensionExamples.example: It is possible for a single player to do all the work but as the quota gets bigger it will become almost impossible for that to happen

dimension.title: Piggy-Backing
dimension.description: Piggy-Backing refers to a specific mechanic, where one player's performance can be leveraged for others to bypass challenges.

dimensionExamples.example: There are two forms of consumables in the game: scrap and money. Scrap can be used to gain money but players can choose ether or not to use them. Money is used to meet the quota and to buy unlockables.

dimension.title: Consumables
dimension.description: Consumables refer to items that exist in a limited amount and can be utilised by players to invoke an effect (usually existing as a form of currency, materials, or food) or are not consumed on purpose by players but support the gameplay (e.g., health, energy). Consumables are shared when the agency to consume and manage them pertains to more than one player.

dimensionExamples.example: Unlockables can be unlocked with money, there are many different unlockables and some can be lost and bought multiple times while others are a one time buy upgrade.

dimension.title: Unlockables
dimension.description: Unlockables refer to content available in the gameplay but not accessible up until players are able and choose to get access to it. Usually, games limit the number of unlocks a player can acquire. Unlockables are shared when the decision to unlock new content pertains to more than one player. The effect of the unlockables may or may not be shared (it might affect only one player, but they would still be shared if more than one player could make the decision).

dimensionExamples.example: Information is the main source of asymmetry in the game. Often times players will go to different places and aquire important information (location of monsters or loot) that is important to be shared. The flow of information is very limited due to the proximity chat used as the main form of communication.

dimension.title: Information
dimension.description: Information, as described by Harris et al. 2016, is where one player knows something other players do not. In cooperative games, this is leveraged by ensuring the information is needed to be shared, or acted upon by more than the player with access to the knowledge. This is typically instantiated with players having Distinct - Player Views and Worlds.

dimensionExamples.example: The main focus of the game is to collect loot, however players can only carry so much. Their teamates are expected to help in finding more loot and carrying it in order to maximaize the team's gain.

dimension.title: Complementarity
dimension.description: Complementarity, extended from Rocha et. al rocha2008game, corresponds to when player actions are designed to balance each other’s weaknesses or so that strengths complement each other. It is typically achieved through asymmetric game design, with each player bringing something to the shared experience.
